notes: Malachi can be read as a personal name or as “my messenger.”
Loved and hated are retained with their force in the contrast between Jacob and Esau; the note does not reduce them to mild preference.
The Hebrew describes the offering with present participial language. The draft leaves its relation to the surrounding future hope open.
vocabulary: The respect due within the father/son and master/servant comparisons.
A fragrant offering associated with worship.

notes: The Hebrew “seed” can refer to offspring or seed for sowing; the draft uses offspring while retaining the ambiguity here.
The wake-and-answer expression is obscure. It is retained as a paired expression rather than turned into a confident identification of two social offices.
The verse’s “one,” remaining spirit, and offspring language is difficult to connect syntactically. The draft preserves the terms and marks the uncertainty rather than claiming a settled argument.

The Hebrew third-person construction is rendered as the man who hates and divorces. “I hate divorce” is another traditional construal; it is not the wording adopted here. The violence image is retained.
vocabulary: The relationship invoked for priestly instruction and responsibility.
Marriage described through a binding relationship to which the LORD is witness.

notes: “My messenger” echoes the name or title at 1:1. The Lord and messenger-of-the-covenant language is retained without assigning each phrase an extra identity.
The relationship between the LORD’s not changing and Jacob’s sons not coming to an end is preserved.
vocabulary: Two images of cleansing that introduce the testing of the priests.
A record image for those who fear the LORD and honor his name.

notes: These public verses are Hebrew 3:19–24. The original source records are bound individually despite the chapter-number difference.
“Wings” belongs to the sun’s healing image. The final destruction term carries the force of a ban; the family reconciliation names fathers and children specifically.
vocabulary: The mountain name used when recalling Moses’s law.
The prophet whose promised coming returns as a question in Matthew 11 and 17.
